name: Castiglione
summary: 5 August 1796, and the everyday case the design is measured against. Wurmser stands across the Castiglione road with his right on the Solferino heights and his left out in the open plain, resting on the entrenched knoll of Monte Medolano — a flank anchored on a hillock and beyond that hanging in the air. Bonaparte has to hold the whole line by the throat long enough for the column coming up from Guidizzolo to walk onto that flank from behind. The Field is a reading of the morainic ground south of Lake Garda rather than a survey of it: hills across the north, plain to the south, and the Redone between the two armies costing a battalion time without funnelling it anywhere.

armies.name: French
armies.brief: Take hold of the whole Austrian line and do not let go of it, because the column coming up from Guidizzolo arrives behind their left twenty minutes in and has to find them still facing you. Marmont's horse battery is the answer to the guns on Monte Medolano, and it will not move until it is hitched up. The knoll is the only ground here that counts at the end.

armies.name: Austrian
armies.brief: Hold the position until the light goes. Your right is on the heights and can look after itself; your left rests on the battery on Monte Medolano and then simply stops, with nothing past it but the road up from Medole. Whatever comes up that road is behind you, and the knoll is the one piece of ground the day is counted on.

chapters.title: Wurmser stands across the road
chapters.text: 5 August 1796. Wurmser has come down from the Tyrol to relieve Mantua and has the Army of Italy in front of him on the plain south of Lake Garda. His right is up on the Solferino heights and can look after itself. His left is out in the open, resting on the entrenched knoll of Monte Medolano — and past the knoll there is nothing at all. Watch the French spread across the whole front: none of it is meant to break through.

chapters.title: Marmont's guns come up
chapters.text: Marmont takes his horse battery forward against the guns on the knoll — what the French brief calls the answer to them. Under these rules it is not much of one: a battery is a poor target for a battery, being few men spread thin, and Monte Medolano will still be firing half an hour from now. What the move actually buys is that the Austrians are looking west.

chapters.title: The 51e pays for the open ground
chapters.text: The 51e breaks with a fifth of its men down, caught crossing a plain in front of two batteries. This is the bill Bonaparte is choosing to pay. He is not trying to win in front of Wurmser — he is trying to hold him by the throat and be expensive enough about it that the Austrian left never turns round.

chapters.title: Fiorella comes up from Guidizzolo
chapters.text: The head of Fiorella's column walks onto the Field behind the Austrian left. This is the whole of the plan for 5 August: a detached force up the Medole road onto a flank that ends in open air. Wurmser now has an enemy on two sides of one corner, and the knoll is what that corner is built on.

chapters.title: Jellačić's battalion gives way
chapters.text: IR 53 breaks. The Austrian left has been fighting west against the grenadiers and south against Fiorella at the same time, and what goes first is not the knoll but the infantry standing round it. A battery with no covering line is about to find out what that is worth.

chapters.title: The knoll is taken
chapters.text: The 1er Hussards ride in on the battery on Monte Medolano and it breaks. What ends a battery is rarely fire — it is horse arriving among the pieces, and 135 gunners in the open have no answer to it. This is the ground the day is counted on, and the French are standing on it from here to dusk.

chapters.title: The Austrian left comes apart
chapters.text: IR 52 quits the Field. Wurmser has now lost the knoll, the battalion behind it and the hussars that covered it. Historically this is about where he broke off and withdrew across the Mincio. Here the clock simply keeps running, because a battle in this game ends when the afternoon does.

chapters.title: What it was worth
chapters.text: Wurmser got away south-east over the Mincio with most of his army, which is what the clock stands for: neither ending here is annihilation. What Castiglione cost him was the initiative in Italy, and Mantua stayed shut.
